You are a blind semantic decoder of a natural-language crystal description. The user message is your only source of material-specific information. Understand the spatial narrative and produce a construction plan; do not guess missing independent numbers or look up a material. Return one JSON object only, without Markdown fences.
For sufficient information use:
{"status":"ok","space_group_number":integer,"hall_symbol":"Hall symbol stated in the text","lattice":[input_a,input_b,input_c,input_alpha,input_beta,input_gamma],"composition":{"Element":input_cell_atom_count},"orbits":[{"element":"Element","wyckoff":"multiplicity_and_letter","representative":[standard_fractional_x,standard_fractional_y,standard_fractional_z]}],"frame_transform":{"matrix":[[p11,p12,p13],[p21,p22,p23],[p31,p32,p33]],"origin_shift":[s1,s2,s3]},"round_digits":integer_or_null,"precision_corrections":[{"element":"Element","at":[input_fractional_x_before_correction,input_fractional_y_before_correction,input_fractional_z_before_correction],"delta":[fractional_dx,fractional_dy,fractional_dz]}]}
Lengths use angstroms, angles use degrees. The specified lattice and composition refer to the original input cell. Orbit representatives refer to the standard Hall coordinate frame. Copy the Hall symbol as a mathematical identifier rather than guessing a public-table integer number. Any equivalent representative of a declared orbit is allowed. Distinct independent orbits of the same element remain separate.
The geometry engine expands the public Hall symmetry orbits, applies q_input = inverse(P)(q_standard - s), selects images in the input cell, rounds fractional coordinates if round_digits is given, and applies precision corrections at their identified input-frame atom positions. If the text explicitly uses identical frames, supply identity P and zero shift. If no rounding is specified, use null. If no corrections are specified, use an empty array. All sites have full occupancy.
Numerical relations in the prose should be resolved into numbers in the plan. Do not silently replace the original geometry with an idealized one. For missing required information return {"status":"insufficient_information","reason":"..."}; for contradictory constraints return {"status":"conflict","reason":"..."}. Your input contains no source CIF or hidden data. Public crystallographic definitions are allowed; material-specific external retrieval is not.

The structure is described in an orthorhombic input cell with lattice parameters a = 6.703341 Å, b = 6.849922 Å, and c = 7.766536 Å, with all three interaxial angles equal to exactly 90.0°. The input cell contains 16 atoms in total, with the declared composition K₄C₄S₄N₄, that is, four potassium, four carbon, four sulfur, and four nitrogen atoms per input cell. The symmetry is that of space group number 57, Pbcm, with Hall symbol −P 2c 2b.

All atomic positions are given as fractional coordinates. The standard crystallographic frame and the input frame are related by q_standard = P q_input + s, where the origin shift s is (0.0, 0.0, 0.0) and the matrix P is, to the stated precision, the permutation that maps an input fractional coordinate (x_in, y_in, z_in) to a standard coordinate (y_in, x_in, −z_in); explicitly, the first row of P is (0.0, 0.9999999999999999, 0.0), the second row is (0.9999999999999999, 1.001338495588927e-33, 0.0), and the third row is (7.983801647119781e-33, −2.7560308570096835e-33, −0.9999999999999999). The tiny departures of the matrix entries from exact 0, 1, and −1 are numerical artifacts at the stated precision, and the origin is unshifted. Coordinate values are reported rounded to six decimal places, and no positional corrections beyond this rounding are required for any atom in this structure.

In the standard frame, the sixteen atoms are arranged on four crystallographically independent orbits, each of multiplicity four, so that each orbit accounts for one quarter of the atoms and together they reproduce the full K₄C₄S₄N₄ content. The potassium ions occupy the Wyckoff position 4c, whose sites have the coordinate form (x, 1/4, 0), with the single free parameter x = 0.198758. Thus one representative potassium atom sits at fractional position (0.198758, 0.25, 0.0), and the remaining three potassium atoms are generated from it by the Pbcm symmetry operations, giving a layer of potassium atoms lying on the mirror plane at z = 0 with their second coordinate fixed at one quarter of the b axis.

The carbon, sulfur, and nitrogen atoms each occupy their own independent 4d orbit, all sharing the coordinate form (x, y, 1/4) but with distinct pairs of free parameters, so that these three species form separate sublattices confined to the plane at z = 1/4. The carbon 4d orbit has free parameters x = 0.231694 and y = 0.787215, placing a representative carbon atom at (0.231694, 0.787215, 0.25). The sulfur 4d orbit has x = 0.395181 and y = 0.610331, with representative position (0.395181, 0.610331, 0.25). The nitrogen 4d orbit has x = 0.111713 and y = 0.916238, with representative position (0.111713, 0.916238, 0.25). For each of these three orbits the Pbcm operations generate four symmetry-equivalent sites from the representative, so that carbon, sulfur, and nitrogen each contribute four atoms distributed over the z = 1/4 plane at their respective (x, y) locations.

Taken together, the structure consists of a potassium sublattice on the 4c sites at z = 0 with y fixed at 1/4 and x ≈ 0.198758, and three chemically distinct but geometrically analogous sublattices of carbon, sulfur, and nitrogen on separate 4d orbits at z = 1/4, distinguished by their independent (x, y) parameters. Applying the inverse of the stated frame transformation to these standard-frame coordinates, with the same orthorhombic input cell dimensions given above, recovers the original input-cell description of this K₄C₄S₄N₄ structure in space group Pbcm.
